To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the unfolded state of proteins is more structured than previously thought, and that the structure and dynamics of the unfolded state of a protein is strongly dependent on the environment in which the protein is found.

the unfolded and partially folded conformations of proteins can be studied by NMR and that these studies provide unique information about the structures, dynamics, and energetics of these conformational states.

the NMR chemical shifts of proteins in unfolded or partially folded states provide information about the secondary structure and dynamics of these states, and that the chemical shift changes upon unfolding or refolding of a protein provide a measure of the changes in secondary structure and dynamics upon folding.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of NMR spectroscopy to study protein folding, structure and function.
the application of NMR to study protein folding and function, and to understand the relationship between structure, dynamics and function in proteins and protein assemblies.
understanding protein folding and function at the molecular level using multidimensional NMR techniques.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the NMR chemical shifts of proteins in the native state are highly sensitive to their three-dimensional structure and can provide a wealth of structural and dynamic information, while in the unfolded and partially folded state they are more sensitive to the local environment of the amino acid residues.
the NMR studies have shown that the unfolded state of a protein has a structure, which is not random.

the equilibrium NMR studies of protein unfolding have provided important insights into the nature of protein structure and the process of protein folding, and have contributed to our understanding of the mechanisms by which proteins function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we use NMR to study protein structure in unfolded states and to understand the role of the unfolded state in folding.
we have used NMR to study the structures and dynamics of proteins in unfolded states and in the partially folded states that occur during the folding process.

the NMR data obtained for unfolded and partially folded peptides and proteins have provided a wealth of information that has been used to develop new models for the structures and dynamics of unfolded and partially unfolded states of proteins and for the mechanism of protein folding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structure of the unfolded state is not as random as previously believed.
NMR can be used as a tool to study proteins in the unfolded and partially folded state and that the structural information gained can be used to understand protein function.
the unfolded state is a dynamic equilibrium ensemble of structures and that this ensemble is a function of the chemical environment of the protein.
